## Introduction

Filtering cells using strict thresholds for features, counts, and mitochondrial 
percentages can remove specific cell types or cell states. Therefore, 
conditional filtering taking complexity information (counts and / or features) 
and mitochondrial percentages into consideration should be prioritized.

[miQC](https://bioconductor.org/packages//release/bioc/html/miQC.html) provides 
a convenient approach overcoming the need for specifying specific cutoffs for
complexity information and mitochondrial percentages by fitting a two-component
mixture model using [flexmix](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=flexmix). 

`miQCadj `provides both an implementation of the original `miQC` classification,
and extends the workflow 

- Featuring [Seurat](https://satijalab.org/seurat/) and [SummarizedExperiment](https://bioconductor.org/packages/SummarizedExperiment/) workflows, 
- Supporting median-based identification of intact and compromised model components for 
spline, polynomial, and polynomial-raw models,
- Enabling comparisons of model classification, original and geometry-based adjustments 
by labeling of compromised cell fractions before transferring the selected results 
back to the input objects.

---

## Running miQCadj using a subset of pbmcsca

This vignette demonstrates the functionality of the `miQCadj` package using 
two small example datasets derived from the pbmcsca dataset provided by the
[SeuratData](https://github.com/satijalab/seurat-data) package.

The included datasets represent peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs)
from two samples processed with different sequencing technologies:

- pbmc1_Smart-seq2  
- pbmc2_CEL-Seq2  

These subsets were selected to illustrate:

- geometry-based reassignment of misclassified cells  
- differences between intercept- and median-based component selection  

The original dataset is available via the [SeuratData](https://github.com/satijalab/seurat-data) package.

---

## Settings & Data

```{r load-data}
library(miQCadj)
library(Seurat)
library(SeuratObject)
library(SingleCellExperiment)
library(ggplot2)
data("pbmc_sub2", package = "miQCadj")
```


The `pbmc_sub2` subset got 33694 genes and 526 cells with 253 cells for pbmc1 
generated with Smartseq2 and 273 cells for pbmc2 generated with CELSeq2:
```{r table-sample-tech}
stats::addmargins(table(pbmc_sub2$sample_tech))
```

The `meta.data` already comprises information regarding the features (`"nFeature_RNA"`),
UMI counts (`"nCount_RNA"`), and mitochondrial percentages (`"percent.mt"`).
Additionally, we have cell type annotation available (`"CellType"`).

Cell filtering should be performed per sample. Therefore, we define each sample, while converting 
pbmc2 into a SummarizedExperiment-related object for demonstration purposes:

```{r define-samples}
pbmc1 <- subset(pbmc_sub2, subset=sample_tech=="pbmc1_Smartseq2")
pbmc2 <- subset(pbmc_sub2, subset=sample_tech=="pbmc2_CELSeq2")
pbmc2 <- Seurat::as.SingleCellExperiment(pbmc2)
```

---

## Default Workflow for linear models

### Fit model

First, we select `pbmc1` generated with Smartseq2 and apply `run_miQCadj()``:

```{r run-pbmc1}
fm1 <- run_miQCadj(pbmc1)
```

By default, `percent.mt` will be selected for mitochondrial percentage 
information and `nFeature_RNA` as complexity column for Seurat objects. 
To use `nCount_RNA` as complexity column, set `complexity_column = "nCount_RNA`.
By default, a linear model (`model_type="linear"`) will be applied and the
component identity will be determined using the fitted intercepts.
Median-based component selection will additionally be available for nonlinear
models, where intercept-based ordering may not adequately represent the fitted 
components across the observed complexity range, as shown in the second part of
the vignette.

---

### Check components

```{r fm1-check-components, fig.height=5, fig.width=11, out.width="95%", fig.align="center", fig.cap="**pbmc1_Smartseq2: miQC Classification and Posterior Probability of a Cell being low Quality**"}
check_miQC_components(flexmix_list = fm1, sample_name = "pbmc1_Smartseq2")
```

---

### Define Classification

Next, we apply define a component selection mode and apply a posterior cutoff. 
We will use the default with `component_selection="intercept"` and `posterior_cutoff= 0.75`:

```{r fm1-define-classification}
fm1 <-  define_classification(flexmix_list = fm1)
```

This will add a column `miQC.keep` with `"keep"` and `"discard"` labels.
Cells with an invalid-component posterior probability above the selected cutoff 
are classified as `"discard"`, cells at or below the cutoff are classified as `"keep"`.

---

### Post-hoc adjustments

Post-hoc adjustments are essential for minimizing model-immanent classifications, 
not favored in filtering of Single Cell Datasets. Very simple scenarios occur in
linear datasets, after the discard line crossed the keep line causing removal of 
high complexity, low mitochondrial reads.

Running `adjust_classifications()` will strongly reduce such model-related 
filtering artifacts. We provide an `original_check` and a `geometry_check`, 
which will both be added to the flexmix data frame by default:


```{r fm1-adjust-classification}
fm1 <-  adjust_classification(flexmix_list = fm1)
```

When uing `adjust_classification()`, the `original_check` will always keep 
cells below the intact cell distribution, while the argument `enforce_left_cutoff`
can either be `TRUE`, which will discard several cells with low or intermediate library
complexity and higher mitochondrial percentage, or `FALSE` which will keep those cells. 

The region-related `geometry_check`	performs curve- and distance-based plausibility adjustments,
but hasn't been benchmarked so far, and therefore, it represents an experimental, heuristic 
adjustment method. So it should be visualized and inspected using `check_miQC_predictions()`,
before being selected and applied.

```{r fm1-check-predictions, fig.height=5, fig.width=12, out.width="95%", fig.align="center", fig.cap="**pbmc1_Smartseq2: Unmodified and Adjusted Cell Predictions**"}
check_miQC_predictions(flexmix_list = fm1, sample_name = "pbmc1_Smartseq2",
                       add_unadjusted_prediction = TRUE,  
                       add_compared_prediction = TRUE,
                       adjustment_method = NULL)
```


Though both adjustment methods use very distinct approaches for reassigning cells, they provide identical predictions for this sample given all shared cells are either labelled as `both_keep` or `both_discard`.

Further diagnostics regarding the specific adjustments made by each adjustment method and the corresponding regions, can be visualized using:

```{r fm1-prediction-details, fig.height=8, fig.width=11, out.width="95%", fig.align="center", fig.cap="**pbmc1_Smartseq2: Original and Adjusted Cell Classification**"}
check_miQC_predictions(flexmix_list = fm1, sample_name = "pbmc1_Smartseq2")
```

By default, the returned list of plots will be combined using patchwork. To 
return a list with each plot being separate accessible, set `combine_plots=FALSE`.

---

### Add back to Seurat object

By default, only the final prediction column will be transferred to `input_obj`. 
Given identical results for both adjustment methods, the final prediction column 
would reveal identical results for any adjustment method selected:

```{r pbmc1-add-to-seurat}
pbmc1 <- add_to_input_obj(flexmix_list = fm1, input_obj = pbmc1, 
                          adjustment_method = "original_check")
```

Within the returned Seurat object, we can check, whether specific cell types are 
discarded more often by creating a table showing the cell counts for each cell type: 

```{r pbmc1-cell-counts}
meta <- as.data.frame(pbmc1@meta.data)
stats::addmargins(table(meta$CellType, meta[["miQC.final_prediction"]]))
```

To obtain percentage information across kept and discarded cells within each cell type, we can create a proportional table: 

```{r pbmc1-cell-prop-counts}
round(prop.table(table(meta$CellType, meta[["miQC.final_prediction"]]), 
                 margin = 1), digits = 3)
```


Also, we can create a plot showing the cell types and removed cells within the feature-percent-mt plot:
```{r pbmc1-cell-type-plot, fig.height=5, fig.width=7, out.width="95%", fig.align="center", fig.cap="**pbmc1_Smartseq2: Cell Prediction status colored by Cell Type**"}
meta$CellType <- as.factor(meta$CellType)
meta[["miQC.final_prediction"]] <- as.factor(meta[["miQC.final_prediction"]])
ggplot2::ggplot(meta, ggplot2::aes(x = nFeature_RNA, 
                                   y = percent.mt, 
                                   colour = CellType, 
                                   shape = miQC.final_prediction)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point() + 
  ggplot2::scale_color_brewer(palette = "Paired") + 
  ggplot2::labs(
    title="pbmc1_Smartseq2: Cell Prediction Status colored by Cell Type") + 
  ggplot2::theme_bw()
```

The dataset contains 14 megakaryocytes (5.53%). The 5th percentile of the number of 
detected genes (`nFeature_RNA`) corresponds to 722.6 genes. Applying this threshold 
would exclude 13 of the 14 megakaryocytes (92.9%), leaving only one cell of this population:

```{r remaining-megakaryocytes-five-percent}
# Calculate the 5th percentile of detected genes
feature_cutoff <- unname(quantile(meta$nFeature_RNA, probs = 0.05))
sum(meta$CellType == "Megakaryocyte" & meta$nFeature_RNA > feature_cutoff)
```

This example illustrates how global percentile-based filtering can disproportionately 
affect specific cell populations, even when only a small fraction of the overall dataset 
is excluded. Therefore, the consequences of QC filtering should be evaluated carefully 
to avoid unintentionally removing large fractions of biologically relevant cell populations.

---

## Median-selection for non-linear models

The `pbmc2` sample uses the Seurat-inherent column names `percent.mt` and 
`nFeature_RNA`, instead of standard naming conventions for SummarizedExperiment-
derived objects, which are `subsets_mito_percent` for mitochondrial percentage
information and `detected` for feature information. Therefore, the column names
need to be specified.

By default, the original miQC package uses the intercept for component definition, which can cause incorrect cell selection, if polynomial or spline models are selected:

```{r fm2-polynomial, fig.height=5, fig.width=11, out.width="95%", fig.align="center", fig.cap="**Intercept component selection for pbmc2_CELSeq2: miQC Classification and Posterior Probabilities of a Cell being low Quality**"}
fm2 <- run_miQCadj(input_obj = pbmc2, percent_mt = "percent.mt", 
                   complexity_column = "nFeature_RNA", 
                   model_type = "polynomial", add_median_selection = TRUE)
check_miQC_components(flexmix_list = fm2, 
                      sample_name = "Intercept-based components for pbmc2_CELSeq2", 
                      combine_plots=TRUE)
```

Using the intercept for component selection in this sample would make incorrect assignments, loosing high-quality cells, but keeping low-quality cells. 

So, we can check the median component selection (`use_median_columns = TRUE`) using:
```{r fm2-check-components-median, fig.height=5, fig.width=11, out.width="95%", fig.align="center", fig.cap="**Median component selection for pbmc2_CELSeq2: miQC Classification and Posterior Probabilities of a Cell being low Quality**"}
check_miQC_components(flexmix_list = fm2, 
                      sample_name = "Median-based components for pbmc2_CELSeq2", 
                      use_median_columns = TRUE)
```

The assignments using medians as component selection mode match our biological expectations with low complexity, but high mitochondrial percentage cells belonging to the compromised component. Therefore, we set `component_selection = "median"`, while using the default posterior threshold (`posterior_cutoff=0.75`): 

```{r fm2-define-classification}
fm2 <-  define_classification(flexmix_list = fm2, 
                              component_selection = "median")
```


Afterwards, we adjusted the classification and check the predictions:

```{r fm2-adjust-classification-check-prediction, fig.height=4.5, fig.width=12, out.width="95%", fig.align="center", fig.cap="**Unmodified and Adjusted Cell Predictions for pbmc2_CELSeq2**"}
fm2 <-  adjust_classification(flexmix_list = fm2)

# check predictions
check_miQC_predictions(flexmix_list = fm2,  sample_name = "pbmc2_CELSeq2",
                       add_unadjusted_prediction = TRUE, 
                       add_compared_prediction = TRUE,
                       adjustment_method = NULL)
```

Apparently, the original and geometry-based adjustment methods produced substantially different classifications for the CEL-Seq2 sample with many cells retained in the geometry_check being discarded by the original_check.

We can check the exact counts using:

```{r fm2-table-check-counts}
addmargins(table(fm2$flexmix_data[["miQC.keep_adj_compared"]]))
```

The strict filtering in the original check is introduced by `enforce_left_cutoff=TRUE`. Since removing 93 cells, corresponding to a cell fraction of 34.1%, shouldn't be performed without further checks, we will set `enforce_left_cutoff=FALSE`. This will keep the `left_cutoff` information available, without forcing extensive filtering decisions without further quality checks being performed:

```{r fm2-adjust-prediction-no-left-cutoff, fig.height=4.5, fig.width=12, out.width="95%", fig.align="center", fig.cap="**Unmodified and Adjusted Cell Predictions for pbmc2_CELSeq2 (without left cutoff)**"}
# adjust classification
fm2 <-  adjust_classification(flexmix_list = fm2, enforce_left_cutoff = FALSE)

# check predictions
check_miQC_predictions(flexmix_list = fm2, sample_name = "pbmc2_CELSeq2",
                       add_unadjusted_prediction = TRUE, 
                       add_compared_prediction = TRUE,
                       adjustment_method = NULL)
```

Now, both adjustment methods provide identical results, with no adjustments made, given all shared cells are either labelled as `both_keep` or `both_discard`.

To check the regions assigned in both adjustment methods we can create the prediction plot for both adjustment methods:

```{r fm2-prediction-details,fig.height=8, fig.width=11, out.width="95%", fig.align="center", fig.cap="**Median-based Component Selection and Region-Adjustments for pbmc2_CELSeq2 (without left cutoff)**"}
check_miQC_predictions(fm2, sample_name = "pbmc2_CELSeq2")
```

---

### Add back to SingleCellExperiment object

After setting `enforce_left_cutoff=FALSE`, both adjustment methods provided identical prediction results. To retain all columns from the flexmix data frame enabling further checks, we can set `transfer_columns = "all"`, enabling further checks, i.e. whether specific cell types occupy specific region compartments:

```{r pbmc2-add-to-sce}
pbmc2 <- add_to_input_obj(flexmix_list = fm2, input_obj = pbmc2,  
                          transfer_columns = "all", 
                          adjustment_method = "geometry_check")
```

Within the returned SingleCellExperiment object, we can check, whether specific
cell types arediscarded more often by creating a table showing the cell counts 
for each cell type: 

```{r pbmc2-cell-counts}
col_data <- as.data.frame(SummarizedExperiment::colData(pbmc2))
stats::addmargins(table(col_data$CellType, col_data[["miQC.final_prediction"]]))
```

To obtain percentage information across kept and discarded cells within each cell type, we can create a proportional table: 

```{r pbmc2-cell-prop-counts}
round(prop.table(table(col_data$CellType, col_data[["miQC.final_prediction"]]), 
                 margin = 1), digits = 3)
```


Or by creating a plot showing the cell types and removed cells within the feature-percent-mt plot:
```{r pbmc2-cell-type-plot, fig.height=5, fig.width=7, out.width="95%", fig.align="center", fig.cap="**pbmc2_CELSeq2: Cell Prediction status colored by Cell Type**"}
col_data$CellType <- as.factor(col_data$CellType)
col_data[["miQC.final_prediction"]] <- as.factor(col_data[["miQC.final_prediction"]])
ggplot2::ggplot(col_data, ggplot2::aes(x = nFeature_RNA, 
                                       y = percent.mt, 
                                       colour = CellType, 
                                       shape = miQC.final_prediction)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point() + ggplot2::scale_color_brewer(palette = "Paired") + 
  ggplot2::labs(
    title="pbmc2_CELSeq2: Cell Prediction Status colored by Cell Type") +
  ggplot2::theme_bw()
```
